design_detail: Systematic review and dose–response meta-analysis of 44 observational studies (32 cohort, 12 case-control; editors' count from Table 1) of average alcohol intake and ischaemic heart disease (IHD), with lifetime abstainers as the reference: former drinkers were excluded, and mortality estimates from studies whose reference group was current non-drinkers were corrected by a fixed factor for former drinking. Continuous dose–response curves were fitted by fractional polynomials (pool-first generalized least squares) and categorical random-effects meta-analyses were run, stratified by sex and end point (IHD mortality, IHD morbidity), first in the 24 studies that reported fully stratified estimates and then in all 44 (adding 20 that reported sex or end point combined). Not registered; MOOSE. Read in the PMC author manuscript.
can_establish: The pooled association between average alcohol intake (up to 72 g/day) and IHD mortality and morbidity, separately for men and women, against lifetime abstainers in published observational studies from 1980 to 2010, and how wide the uncertainty is at about one to three drinks a day once sex and end point are kept apart.
cannot_establish: Whether drinking lowers IHD risk (observational studies, a quarter adjusted for age only, residual confounding acknowledged by the authors); the role of drinking pattern (not analysed, and named by the authors as a likely source of the unexplained heterogeneity); risk above 72 g/day (excluded); and whether lifetime abstainers are a fair comparison group (their health and social characteristics were not examined).

sample.recruitment: Search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science (Science Citation Index Expanded, Social Sciences Citation Index, Arts & Humanities Citation Index) from January 1980 to the second week of April 2010, without language restriction and excluding letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments, plus relevant reviews, meta-analyses and the references of identified papers (Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph). The pooled studies are cohorts and case-control studies of general or occupational populations, 16 from the USA, 5 from Japan, 4 from the UK and 19 from New Zealand, Australia, Denmark, Sweden, Italy, other European countries, Costa Rica and China (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1); samples of high-risk populations only were excluded.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case-control or cohort studies reporting a relative-risk measure with its variability (or data to compute them) for IHD as a separate outcome (ICD-9 410–414, ICD-10 I20–I25); at least three intake categories among current drinkers; a reference period of more than 2 weeks for average intake, determined from usual frequency and usual volume or from the number of drinks in the period; estimates at least age-adjusted. Excluded: semi-quantitative food-frequency questionnaires combining frequency and volume in one ambiguous question; qualitative labels such as problem or social drinkers; self-reported IHD morbidity; cardiovascular outcomes combined with stroke; samples of high-risk populations only. Estimates adjusted for blood pressure or cholesterol (treated as mediators) were avoided where another was available (Methods › Search strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Table 1 gives each study's end point, sex, design, number of cases (34 to 6,135), total sample size (309 to 245,207), country and covariates; age at baseline and follow-up are not given per study. Mean age at the time of the IHD event per stratum was 56 to 67 years (Table 3). The case-control studies contributed 9,846 cases and 13,199 controls; the cohorts 6,942 events with end points combined and 21,839 end point-specific events among 934,639 people (Results, 2nd paragraph). Only two studies gave estimates for a race other than white.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.
sample.selection_effects: One author screened titles and abstracts. The criteria select studies with at least three drinking categories and adequate intake measurement, which the authors say were partly driven by practicality. Most studies come from high-income countries. The fully stratified analyses for women rest on 5 to 8 studies, and women's morbidity mainly on case-control studies: of the six Table 1 studies giving stratified estimates for women with a morbidity end point, five are case-control (editors' reading of Table 1). Conference abstracts and other grey literature were excluded. Six of the 24 fully stratified studies are case-control studies (Kaufman 1985, Scragg 1987, Jackson 1991, Romelsjö 2003, Tavani 2004, Dorn 2007), all contributing estimates of new cases (Scragg also of deaths), so the stratified morbidity estimates rest substantially on case-control data (editors' count from Table 1). Freedom from heart disease at the start was not an inclusion criterion: only samples made up entirely of high-risk people were excluded, and some included studies adjusted for prior disease (for example McElduff 1997: angina, stroke and previous myocardial infarction; Doll 1994: history of previous disease).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported average intake at baseline (cohorts) or before the event (case-control studies) over a reference period of more than 2 weeks, from frequency and quantity or from drinks per period. The reviewers converted categories to g/day at their midpoints, added three quarters of the previous category to the lower bound of open-ended categories, and used reported or standard conversion factors (WHO, 2000) where intake was in drinks; several estimates per stratum from one article were combined by fixed effects so that each article gave at most one curve per stratum (Methods › Data extraction and synthesis).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categorical analysis: lifetime abstainers (reference); occasional drinkers, defined in the Methods as less than weekly drinking or 0.1–2.49 g/day and in the table footnotes as less than 1 drink a week or under 2.5 g/day; 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99 and 24–35.99 g/day, read as about 1, 2 and 3 standard drinks of 12 g. Continuous analysis up to 72 g/day; people drinking more than 72 g/day were excluded for scarcity of data. Drinking pattern was not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only through primary-study adjustment: smoking appears in many but not all models in Table 1, and 11 of 44 studies adjusted for age alone (editors' count). Other drug use not addressed.

comparison.controls: Lifetime abstainers. Former drinkers were excluded from all analyses. Where a study's reference group was current non-drinkers, its mortality estimates were corrected for the former drinkers in that group using the authors' earlier meta-analysis (men: former-drinker relative risk 1.25 and a mean former-drinker fraction of 0.32 among current non-drinkers; women: 1.54 and 0.08), on the log scale; morbidity estimates were not corrected because former drinkers' morbidity risk did not differ significantly from lifetime abstainers'. Where the reference was, for example, light drinkers, estimates were recalculated against abstainers (Methods › Data extraction and synthesis). The paper does not say how many studies had current non-drinkers as their reference, so the lifetime-abstainer estimates of Tables 2 and 4 combine true lifetime-abstainer comparisons, mortality estimates corrected for former drinkers and, for new cases, uncorrected comparisons whose reference included former drinkers.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Health and social characteristics of lifetime abstainers; the authors say strict control for smoking and baseline health status, or longer reference periods, would have left too few studies (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph). Eleven of 44 studies adjusted only for age. The fixed correction assumes the same former-drinker share and excess risk in every study and country.

outcomes.instruments: IHD mortality or morbidity (ICD-9 410–414; ICD-10 I20–I25) as ascertained by each study; self-reported morbidity excluded (Methods › Search strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias tool was applied to the included studies; quality was handled through the eligibility criteria (exposure measurement, minimum age adjustment, exclusion of high-risk samples) and meta-regression on adjustment.
outcomes.operationalization: Hazard ratios, relative risks and odds ratios all treated as relative risks. The continuous curves are summarized by the nadir (intake of lowest risk) and the reversion point (where the curve turns into a detrimental association), both in g/day and without confidence intervals.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four strata (men's and women's IHD mortality and morbidity), each with continuous models in two study sets (8 models, Table 3), 32 categorical pooled estimates (Tables 2 and 4) and 6 subgroup estimates (Table 5), plus meta-regression on four study characteristics.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. One author performed the search and the first exclusion pass on titles and abstracts; studies identified for detailed assessment were discussed and agreed by both authors without blinding to study characteristics. Who extracted the data, and whether in duplicate, is not stated (Methods › Search strategy, 2nd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Fractional-polynomial dose–response curves (powers −2 to 3, one turning point) by the pool-first method of Greenland and Longnecker and Orsini et al.; categorical DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling after fixed-effect pooling within studies; Cochran's Q and I² with 95% CIs; Peters' test for publication bias; leave-one-out sensitivity analysis; meta-regression on age at the event (under 65 or 65 and over), age-only adjustment and adjustment for blood pressure or cholesterol, and on design for men's morbidity only (Methods › Statistical analysis). All estimates against lifetime abstainers. Fully stratified studies (Table 2), at 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99 and 24–35.99 g/day: men's IHD mortality 0.89 (0.79 to 1.00), 0.86 (0.73 to 1.02), 0.78 (0.63 to 0.97); men's morbidity 0.77 (0.65 to 0.92), 0.75 (0.64 to 0.88), 0.74 (0.53 to 1.02); women's mortality 0.84 (0.74 to 0.96), 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27), 0.89 (0.57 to 1.40); women's morbidity 0.54 (0.45 to 0.65), 0.61 (0.38 to 0.99), 0.40 (0.14 to 1.13). All 44 studies (Table 4): estimates from 0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1. Nadirs in fully stratified studies (Table 3): 32 g/day for men's mortality (reversion 63), 69 for men's morbidity, 11 for women's mortality (reversion 31), 14 for women's morbidity (reversion 57). I² 46 to 59% for the curves and up to 84% for the categories.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; estimates had to be at least age-adjusted, and estimates not adjusted for blood pressure or cholesterol were preferred. Meta-regression found no effect of age-only adjustment or of adjustment for blood pressure or cholesterol, and the results were reported as confirmed in studies not adjusted for these intermediates (no numbers given; Results › Categorical meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review followed the MOOSE guidelines (Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives no numerical results; it says some cardioprotective association was confirmed in all strata, with wide intervals at 1–2 drinks a day. The non-significant stratified estimates for men's mortality at about 1 and 2 drinks and for women's mortality at about 2 drinks (1.03) are in Table 2 and the text but not in the abstract. The sensitivity analysis excluding mediator-adjusted estimates and the non-significant meta-regressions are reported only in words.
analysis.power: The authors state that power to identify sources of heterogeneity was low; several stratified categories rest on 2 or 3 studies (women's occasional drinking and morbidity, 2; men's and women's morbidity at 24–35.99 g/day, 3 each; occasional drinking in men's morbidity and women's mortality, 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against lifetime abstainers, IHD risk curves by average intake were J-shaped or levelled off in all four sex-by-end point strata, with nadirs from 11 g/day (women's mortality) to 69 g/day (men's morbidity) in fully stratified studies. In the categorical analysis of those studies, men's IHD mortality was not significantly lower at about 1 drink (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00) or 2 drinks a day (0.86, 0.73 to 1.02), only at about 3 (0.78, 0.63 to 0.97); women's mortality was lower at about 1 drink (0.84) but not at 2 (1.03). Morbidity estimates at about 1 to 3 drinks were lower (0.40 to 0.77), most strongly for women (0.54 at about 1 drink, from 5 mostly case-control studies). Adding the studies that combined sexes or end points gave significant reductions at about 1 to 3 drinks in every stratum (relative risks 0.62 to 0.81). Occasional drinking was not associated with IHD in any stratum. Heterogeneity was substantial and largely unexplained.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract is cautious and matches the results: it concludes that a cardioprotective association cannot be assumed for all drinkers, even at low intake. The body is less consistent. (1) The implications state that most of the cardioprotective effect is already reached at 1–2 drinks a day for men and 1 for women, and that the findings support current low-risk drinking guidelines, although the stratified men's mortality estimates at about 1 and 2 drinks were not significant; effect is causal language the design cannot support (Discussion › Implications, 5th paragraph). (2) They place the men's nadirs at 33 to 69 g/day with a significant effect in both the continuous and the categorical analyses, but the categorical analysis stops at 36 g/day and its stratified men's-morbidity estimate at 24–35.99 g/day was not significant (0.74, 0.53 to 1.02) (Implications, 1st paragraph). (3) The discussion calls some form of cardioprotective association hard to deny and treats short-term biomarker trials as perhaps the strongest argument for causality, while the limitations say residual confounding cannot be excluded and may bias in either direction. (4) Confounding other than by age is called usually small on the strength of another review (Ronksley et al., 2011), not of an analysis in this one. On balance the paper's own uncertainty statements are prominent and accurate; the overreach is confined to parts of the implications.

timeline.event: Fillmore et al. (Addiction Research & Theory), systematic error in prospective studies of moderate drinking: among the meta-analyses scrutinized for references (ref. 27).

Roerecke & Rehm (American Journal of Epidemiology), irregular heavy drinking occasions and IHD: relative risk 1.45 (1.24 to 1.70) for drinkers with such occasions against those without (cited in the implications, ref. 29).
Roerecke & Rehm (American Journal of Epidemiology), IHD in former drinkers: the source of this review's correction factors (ref. 36).

Ronksley et al. (BMJ), criticized in this review's introduction for comparing drinkers with current non-drinkers, so ignoring former drinkers, and for not reporting intake-specific risks by sex against lifetime abstainers (read in this round; card sc_ronksley_2011).
This review: J-shaped or levelling curves against lifetime abstainers in every stratum, but non-significant associations at about 1–2 drinks a day for men's IHD mortality in fully stratified studies.

Roerecke & Rehm (BMC Medicine) summarize this review as showing a clearly beneficial association against lifetime abstainers, citing its all-studies estimates of 0.69 to 0.81 at 1–2 drinks a day without its non-significant stratified estimates for men's mortality (read in this round; card sc_roerecke_2014).

Holmes et al. (BMJ) Mendelian randomization analysis, described by Roerecke & Rehm (2014) as finding no protective effect of alcohol on IHD; on the Tier A list with later genetic studies, read in this round by another reader.

replication.where_it_stands: This is the meta-analysis that keeps sex and end point apart against lifetime abstainers. Its stratified results show how fragile the association at 1–2 drinks a day is for men's IHD mortality, while its all-studies results are the ones its authors later quote. Genetic studies (Holmes et al., 2014, and later) challenge the causal interpretation. Claims should cite the stratified and the all-studies estimates side by side, each with its reference group (lifetime abstainers) and end point.

funding.funder: A small contribution from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study, and the NIAAA grant Drinking Patterns & Ethnicity: Impact on Mortality Risks (1R01AA016644-01A1) to the second author (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: J. Rehm declares that he has taken part in scientific meetings organized or sponsored by the alcohol industry and received financial support for this participation, and that his research has been funded by governments, national scientific research funds, the National Institutes of Health, the Canadian Institutes for Health Research, other public-health agencies in Australia, Austria, Canada, Germany and the United States, and international organizations. All other authors declare no interests (Acknowledgments; Declarations of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto; Rehm also at the Technische Universität Dresden. Rehm is an author of two included studies (Rehm 1997, ref. 78; Sempos 2002, ref. 49), and the former-drinker correction rests on the authors' own 2011 meta-analysis. The alcohol-industry meeting support is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Individual-participant data from cohorts with lifetime drinking histories that separate lifetime abstainers, former and occasional drinkers, with repeated measures of intake and drinking pattern and pre-baseline health status, analysed by sex and end point; together with genetic analyses able to estimate the shape of the curve at low intake. A long-term randomized trial would settle causation but is not in prospect.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (general-population samples, high-risk samples excluded), exposure (average intake by level), comparator (lifetime abstainers), outcome (IHD mortality and morbidity by ICD codes) and designs are specified.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Case-control and cohort studies; the discussion explains that long-term randomized trials are lacking for ethical and logistical reasons (Discussion › Implications, 3rd paragraph).

Three databases with the full search string and no language restriction, plus reference lists of reviews and identified papers; but letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments were excluded and the search began in 1980, without a stated reason, and no grey literature, registries or experts were consulted. Under the project's reading of item 4 (decision of 25 October), an unjustified restriction on publication type is judged no.
One author performed the search and excluded studies at the first pass on titles and abstracts; only the detailed assessment was agreed by both authors.
Who extracted the data, and whether two people did, is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 (an image) shows the flow from 392 full papers to 44 articles; no list of excluded studies with reasons is given.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives end point, sex, design, cases, sample size, country and covariates for each study; age, follow-up, exposure instrument and type of reference group are not given per study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No study-level appraisal of risk of bias. Quality was handled by eligibility criteria that still admit age-only adjustment (11 of 44 studies) and case-control studies without appraisal of control selection or recall. A lenient reading could give partial yes for the attention to confounding (minimum age adjustment, avoidance of mediator adjustment) and to selection of the reference group (former drinkers excluded or corrected); the overall rating is the same either way.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Pool-first fractional-polynomial models take account of the correlation of categories within a study; categorical estimates were pooled by random effects after within-study fixed-effect pooling; only adjusted (at least age-adjusted) estimates were combined, and mediator-adjusted estimates were avoided where possible. Weaknesses: the former-drinker correction is one fixed factor for all studies, with no stated allowance for its uncertainty; case-control odds ratios and cohort relative risks are combined; nadirs and reversion points have no intervals, and the authors themselves say the continuous intervals overstate precision at low intake. Judged met on balance because the categorical analysis was added to show that uncertainty.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Meta-regression on age-only adjustment and on adjustment for blood pressure or cholesterol, a restriction to studies without mediator adjustment, and a test of design for men's morbidity examine bias-related features, although there was no risk-of-bias rating to stratify by.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations discuss residual confounding, misclassification of drinking over time and the practical compromises in the eligibility criteria, and the abstract's conclusion is limited accordingly; parts of the implications depart from this (see interpretation gap).

I² with confidence intervals and Q for every pooled estimate; meta-regression on four characteristics and a subgroup analysis by age for women's mortality; the unexplained heterogeneity is discussed and drives the conclusion that cardioprotection cannot be assumed for all drinkers.

Peters' test for every categorical estimate (one of the 31 tested significant: women's mortality at 12–23.99 g/day in fully stratified studies, P=0.01) and leave-one-out analyses; discussed only briefly.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the second author's interests, including support for attending alcohol-industry-sponsored meetings, are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, unjustified restriction on publication types; 7, excluded studies; 9, study-level risk of bias), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; items 11, 13 and 15 are met. Single-author screening and undocumented extraction add to the risk that studies or numbers were missed. In its favour, the review keeps sex and end point apart, removes former drinkers from the reference group, uses appropriate dose–response methods, reports heterogeneity and a publication-bias test for every estimate, and states its own uncertainty plainly. Its numbers can be cited as what published studies to 2010 show against lifetime abstainers, with the stratified and all-studies estimates side by side; they cannot be cited as effects of drinking. Several internal inconsistencies of the author manuscript (reporting issues) could not be checked against the version of record.

key_findings.finding: Search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science from January 1980 to April 2010, without language restriction: 1,538 unique citations, 392 full papers retrieved, 44 articles included; 32 cohort and 12 case-control studies (editors' count from Table 1).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The analyses used 38,627 IHD events among 957,684 participants: 9,846 cases and 13,199 controls in case-control studies, and 6,942 events with end points combined plus 21,839 end point-specific events among 934,639 people in cohorts. Cases per study 34 to 6,135; sample sizes 309 to 245,207; 16 studies from the USA, 5 from Japan, 4 from the UK. 24 articles gave sex- and end point-specific estimates (the main analyses); 20 gave estimates with sex or end point combined.

Adjustment in the primary studies: 11 of the 44 studies adjusted for age only (editors' count from Table 1); the authors note that a substantial number adjusted only for age, sometimes to avoid adjusting for blood pressure or cholesterol as intermediates.

Former drinkers were excluded; where the reference group was current non-drinkers, mortality estimates were corrected on the log scale using a former-drinker relative risk of 1.25 and a former-drinker fraction of 0.32 among current non-drinkers for men, and 1.54 and 0.08 for women, taken from the authors' 2011 meta-analysis; morbidity estimates were not corrected; intakes above 72 g/day were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data extraction and synthesis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, on our reading of the Methods: the correction multiplies current drinkers' relative risks by about 1.07 for men and 1.04 for women. The Methods' wording of the correction is partly garbled (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Continuous dose–response curves against lifetime abstainers, fully stratified studies: men's IHD mortality nadir 32 g/day, reversion point 63 g/day (17 studies, I² 51%); men's morbidity nadir 69 g/day, no reversion within the range (9 studies, I² 46%); women's mortality nadir 11 g/day, reversion 31 g/day (8 studies, I² 56%); women's morbidity nadir 14 g/day, reversion 57 g/day (5 studies, I² 58%). With all 44 studies: nadirs 37, 72, 23 and 29 g/day (34, 28, 18 and 17 studies), reversion only for women's mortality (62 g/day); I² 46 to 59%.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Continuous dose-response meta-analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text gives the men's mortality nadir as 31 g/day and the implications as 33 g/day (see reporting issues). Nadirs and reversion points have no confidence intervals; the curves (Figures 2 and 3) are images and were not read for values.

key_findings.finding: Categorical analysis against lifetime abstainers, fully stratified studies, men: IHD mortality, occasional drinking 0.94 (0.74 to 1.21), 5 studies; 2.5–11.99 g/day 0.89 (0.79 to 1.00), 17; 12–23.99 g/day 0.86 (0.73 to 1.02), 12; 24–35.99 g/day 0.78 (0.63 to 0.97), 11. IHD morbidity: 0.82 (0.65 to 1.02), 3; 0.77 (0.65 to 0.92), 9; 0.75 (0.64 to 0.88), 8; 0.74 (0.53 to 1.02), 3.
key_findings.note: The authors read 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99 and 24–35.99 g/day as about 1, 2 and 3 standard drinks of 12 g.

key_findings.finding: Categorical analysis against lifetime abstainers, fully stratified studies, women: IHD mortality, occasional 0.98 (0.74 to 1.30), 3 studies; 2.5–11.99 g/day 0.84 (0.74 to 0.96), 8; 12–23.99 g/day 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27), 7; 24–35.99 g/day 0.89 (0.57 to 1.40), 5. IHD morbidity: 0.91 (0.78 to 1.07), 2; 0.54 (0.45 to 0.65), 5; 0.61 (0.38 to 0.99), 5; 0.40 (0.14 to 1.13), 3.
key_findings.note: Women's morbidity strata total only 8,007 people, with high case proportions, consistent with mainly case-control data (editors' arithmetic from Table 2).

key_findings.finding: Categorical analysis against lifetime abstainers, all 44 studies (including estimates with sex or end point combined), at occasional, 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99 and 24–35.99 g/day: men's mortality 0.90 (0.76 to 1.08), 0.81 (0.74 to 0.90), 0.74 (0.66 to 0.84), 0.74 (0.63 to 0.86) (10, 34, 26 and 20 studies); men's morbidity 0.87 (0.75 to 1.01), 0.77 (0.69 to 0.86), 0.70 (0.63 to 0.77), 0.66 (0.57 to 0.76); women's mortality 0.97 (0.84 to 1.11), 0.77 (0.70 to 0.84), 0.74 (0.60 to 0.90), 0.67 (0.56 to 0.80); women's morbidity 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02), 0.70 (0.62 to 0.78), 0.69 (0.56 to 0.84), 0.62 (0.50 to 0.77).

In the authors' reading, confidence intervals from the continuous models overstate precision at about 1–3 drinks a day, and in the categorical analysis the evidence of a cardioprotective association for IHD mortality was borderline at 1–3 drinks a day in both sexes, with upper confidence limits close to or above 1; occasional drinking was not significantly associated with IHD in any stratum.

Heterogeneity was substantial in most analyses (I² up to 84% in Table 2 and 74% in Table 4) and significant in all continuous models; only one pooled categorical estimate showed evidence of publication bias by Peters' test (women's mortality at 12–23.99 g/day, fully stratified, P=0.01), and leaving out studies one at a time did not change any pooled estimate substantially.

Meta-regression: of the study characteristics tested, only age at the IHD event modified the association, for women's mortality. Fully stratified studies, women's IHD mortality: under 65 years, 0.78 (0.60 to 1.00), 0.93 (0.59 to 1.46) and 0.69 (0.20 to 2.42) at about 1, 2 and 3 drinks (4, 3 and 3 studies); 65 years and over, 0.87 (0.72 to 1.05), 1.00 (0.68 to 1.47) and 0.95 (0.68 to 1.32) (4, 4 and 2 studies). No design effect for men's morbidity (likelihood-ratio test p=0.57, 2 df); results reported as confirmed in studies not adjusted for blood pressure or cholesterol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Categorical meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 5; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that advising individuals to start drinking for health cannot be supported, that 1–2 drinks a day should not be seen as a safe level, and that neither taking up drinking for health nor abstinence for low-level drinkers who control their drinking should be promoted; they also state that most of the cardioprotective association is reached at 1–2 drinks a day for men and 1 for women, and that intakes below 1–2 drinks a week do not seem to confer substantial cardioprotection.
key_findings.note: These are the authors' conclusions, appraised in the interpretation gap; the second statement is not supported by the stratified results for men's mortality.

key_findings.finding: The authors cite their 2010 meta-analysis for a relative risk of 1.45 (1.24 to 1.70) for drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them, and suggest that such occasions, which this review could not examine, may explain part of the unexplained heterogeneity.

reporting_issues.issue: The nadir of the men's IHD mortality curve in fully stratified studies is 31 g/day in the results text, 32 g/day in Table 3, and part of a range of 33 to 69 g/day in the implications.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Continuous dose-response meta-analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Discussion › Implications, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The same value appears three ways in the author manuscript; claims should use Table 3 (32 g/day) and say it has no confidence interval.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is titled as describing 43 studies, but it lists 44, and the abstract and results give 44 articles.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; 44 is consistent with the rest of the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4, women's mortality at 24–35.99 g/day has I² 32% with a 95% interval of 43 to 67, which does not contain its own point estimate; the P value of 0.15 with 10 studies is consistent with an I² of about 32% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval is misprinted (its lower limit is probably 0); the I² value itself is usable.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5, the I² values for 12–23.99 g/day do not fit their P values: under 65 years, 3 studies with P=0.63 imply Q of about 0.9 and I² of 0, but I² is printed as 40%; 65 and over, 4 studies with P=0.17 imply Q of about 5.0 and I² of about 40%, but I² is printed as 0 (editors' calculation from the chi-square distribution). The two values appear transposed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Heterogeneity figures for this subgroup should not be cited; the pooled relative risks are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4, the total sample size of men's mortality at 12–23.99 g/day is printed as 588,135, which makes the five men's-mortality categories sum to 1,114,004 people, more than the 957,684 participants of the whole meta-analysis (editors' arithmetic); within one stratum each participant should be counted once.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 4 (men, mortality, 12–23.99 g/day); Abstract (Results)
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is probably misprinted; sample sizes from Table 4 should not be quoted for this category.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2, men's mortality has 16 studies in the lifetime-abstainer reference row but 17 in the 2.5–11.99 g/day category (and 17 in Table 3), although every estimate is expressed against lifetime abstainers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unexplained; perhaps one study's reference group was corrected or recalculated rather than lifetime abstainers, but the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results' sentence that only three studies reported average intakes of 3 or more drinks a day comes directly after the women's results and fits women's morbidity (3 studies at 24-35.99 g a day in Table 2) but not women's mortality (5), so it is best read as being about the women's strata; and the Discussion's statement that all models except women's mortality showed substantial unexplained heterogeneity fits the categorical women's-mortality estimates in Table 2 (heterogeneity P = 0.24, 0.40 and 0.10) but not the continuous women's-mortality curve in Table 3 (I² 56%, P = 0.014).
